name: Sasanian Empire (Khosrow II)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 2.60-2.96 million km2 for 600 CE (low to mid). The historical-basemaps world_600 polygons measure 3.20 million km2 ("Sasanian Empire") + 0.34 million km2 ("Sasanian dependencies", Yemen, a Sasanian province since c. 570) on the sphere, computed from the GeoJSON (high).

population.note: Seshat (Sasanid Empire II) codes 12.7 million for 551-619 CE (mid), 8.9 million for 499-550 (low ~9 million) and 22.1 million for 620-642 when the occupied Roman East was included. High 18 million allows for a larger Mesopotamian population than Seshat assumes. Everything inside the border incl. Mesopotamia, Khuzestan, the plateau, Khorasan, Persarmenia and Yemen; Lakhmid and Arab client tribes outside.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Mesopotamia and Khuzestan were heavily urbanised (Seshat largest settlement Ctesiphon 400,000-500,000 for 499-642, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/130), the plateau and the east much less; set below the late Roman East.

activePersonnel.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 69-72: standing professional army c. 588-603 = 70,000 savaran on the warrior-caste rolls (al-Tabari's 70,000, reinterpreted; Mas'udi has Khosrow II review 50,000 horse c. 603) + ~50,000 (max 60,000) regular infantry (Daylamites, tirbad archers), i.e. ~120,000; plus vassal contingents in service (up to 30,000) and support. Howard-Johnston 1995 (cited by Soto p. 63) estimated ~180,000 for Khosrow I (high side). Counted here: savaran, regular infantry, vassal light horse on duty, garrison levies and support. The peasant levy (paighan) is in trainedReserves. Low allows for a smaller warrior roll after the 589-591 civil war.

trainedReserves.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 73-74: the Chronicle of 1234 gives 120,000 "peasants" with Khosrow I before Dara in 573; Soto puts the ceiling of the paighan levy at ~150,000 (high), usable only for short campaigns. Mid assumes about half can be raised within a campaign season; untrained, but counted here per the levies-in-reserves convention.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Grooms, baggage train, elephant mahouts and crews, engineers, staff and the small Gulf flotilla crews; no source gives a figure.

mobilizationRatio.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 72-74: in great need and for a limited time Persia could field at most ~300,000 men (70,000 savaran, 50,000 regular infantry, 30,000 vassal troops, 150,000 peasant levies, paighan). 300,000 / 12.7 million = 0.024 (mid); low and high bracket a smaller levy and a larger population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 69-70: 70,000 savaran on the rolls in 588 (high); attested single-front concentrations of 15,000 (531), 23,000 and 40,000 (573), and 50,000 horse at Khosrow II's review. Mid 60,000 allows for losses in the civil war of 589-591 and nobles on garrison duty counted as unavailable.

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: lamellar/mail-armoured lancer-archers on armoured horses, the model the Romans copied (clibanarii); era best with the Roman bucellarii.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: hereditary warrior caste trained from youth, periodic royal reviews (Soto p. 69-70 on the 40-day reviews).

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 72-73: vassal contingents (Lakhmid Arabs, Armenian, Albanian and Iberian nobles, settled Hephthalites and Turks) never exceeded ~30,000 in all (high); the largest single contingent was ~15,000 Lakhmids in 531. Mid assumes half on call in peacetime 600.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: horse archers and Arab lancers, lighter kit than the savaran.

training.note: Steppe and Arab horsemen raised in the saddle; not drilled as units.

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 70-71: regular infantry of ~50,000 (max 60,000); the Chronicle of 1234 has 40,000 foot at Dara in 573. Split ~60/40 between shielded close-order infantry (Daylamites, highland peoples; 3,000-4,000-man contingents attested in 554, 573, 642) and archers.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Daylamite medium infantry with shields, swords, axes and javelins; generally lighter than Roman line infantry.

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 70-71: the archer share of the ~50,000 regular infantry (tirbad-led companies; 4,000 archers won at Anglon in 542).
Educated guess. Paighan levies kept under arms in peacetime 600 as garrison and labour troops; the bulk of the levy is in trainedReserves.

quality.note: Rubric 0.25: wicker shield, spear, sometimes sling or sword (Soto p. 73, citing Farrokh).

count.note: Educated guess. Elephants came from India and the corps was "at no time very numerous"; Arabic tradition (al-Tabari, ancient, not fetched) puts about thirty at al-Qadisiyya (636). Khosrow II's legendary stables of several hundred are not used.

quality.note: Indian elephants with towers and armour; effective in sieges and against cavalry, vulnerable to disciplined infantry.

count.note: Educated guess. Siege engines, rams, towers and ballistae used at Amida, Dara and Antioch; no count survives.

training.note: Engineers attached to the royal army.

count.note: Educated guess. Persian Gulf flotilla (the 570 Yemen expedition went by sea; Mas'udi has Khosrow II review army and fleet, as cited by Soto p. 70). No war fleet in the Mediterranean.

quality.note: Sewn-plank and coastal craft, not purpose-built war galleys.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: experienced generals (Bahram Chobin, Shahrbaraz, Shahin) and a structured command (spahbeds of the four quarters), but the 589-591 civil war had just removed or alienated leading commanders.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: savaran loyal to their noble houses; Bahram Chobin's revolt split the army in 589-591 and Khosrow II was restored only with Roman help.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: peace with Rome since 591; elite cavalry confident, levies unwilling.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 plus refinements: heavy composite bows, lance and mace cavalry, stirrups arriving c. 600; below anchor 4 (crossbow, counterweight trebuchet).

armor.note: Above anchor 3 (mail): lamellar and mail with horse armour for the savaran; short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail.

ships.note: Anchor 3 lower end: coastal and Gulf craft, no oared war fleet.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 plus long frontier walls (Gorgan ~195 km, Derbent) and fortified cities (Nisibis, Ctesiphon).

logistics.note: Anchor 3: royal roads and depots, irrigated Mesopotamian granaries; levies limited by agricultural calendar (Soto p. 73-74).

communications.note: Anchor 3: mounted relay posts on the royal roads (later the Abbasid barid).

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts, spies, frontier informants.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true (2011 int$): Iran and Iraq year 1 CE = 1,116; Iraq 730 CE = 1,466 (early Abbasid). Late Sasanian Mesopotamia was the richest irrigated region of the empire; the plateau and Khorasan poorer. Mid ~1,050.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Savaran were partly paid (Khosrow I's reforms introduced state pay and equipment) and partly supported by land; levies unpaid (Soto p. 73).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy with silk weaving, metalwork and caravan trade.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian (Sawad) agriculture produced large tax surpluses; the plateau far less.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads inherited from the Achaemenids and Parthians (Ctesiphon-Hamadan-Rayy-Nishapur-Merv, Ctesiphon-Istakhr); total length not documented.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Ubulla, Rev-Ardashir, Siraf, Hormuz on the Gulf; the river ports of Ctesiphon.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf and Indian Ocean shipping (Persian merchants dominated the Ceylon trade per Procopius); no tonnage figure exists.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1) for infantry armies, extended for a cavalry army living off grazing; Sasanian field armies operated ~1-3 weeks from Mesopotamian bases.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.08-0.14 horses, camels, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population (horse-breeding nobility, Mesopotamian camels).

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: local supply and fortified cities with population support; the plateau gives depth and an arid climate (1.3 at most), but Heraclius showed in 624-628 that the Mesopotamian core was reachable.

notes: Snapshot = 600 CE, Khosrow II (590-628) between his restoration with Roman help (591) and the great war against Rome (603-628). Force convention: activePersonnel = standing savaran heavy cavalry, regular infantry, vassal contingents on duty, garrison levies and support; the peasant levy (paighan) is in trainedReserves. Army figures follow Soto Chica 2015 (Gladius 35), the most detailed source-based reconstruction; medieval Arabic and Persian figures (al-Tabari, Mas'udi, Firdausi) and the Chronicle of 1234 are ancient and are only used through Soto's critique. Border is the historical-basemaps world_600 Sasanian Empire plus "Sasanian dependencies" (Yemen). Lakhmid al-Hira was a client kingdom until 602 and its population is not counted; its horsemen are in cavalry_light. Elephant, ship and siege-engine counts are educated guesses.
